subject: Computer Networking
title: Starlink and Satellite Internet
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Starlink and Satellite Internet.

hook.text: Traditional satellites orbit 36,000 km up. Latency is terrible. SpaceX asked: what if satellites were much closer?

buildup.text: Starlink places thousands of small satellites in low Earth orbit — just 550 km up. Lower orbit means lower latency.

discovery.text: The constellation hands off your connection as satellites pass overhead at 27,000 km/h. Seamless and automatic.

twist.text: Starlink serves areas fiber can't reach economically. It complements city broadband rather than competing with it.

climax.text: Amazon's Kuiper and OneWeb are launching competing constellations. A new space race for internet access is underway.

punchline.text: Satellite internet went from slow backup to legitimate broadband.

quiz.question: Why does Starlink have lower latency than traditional satellite internet?
options: Its satellites orbit much closer to Earth

details.summary: SpaceX's Starlink launched in 2020 to provide global broadband from a low-Earth orbit satellite constellation.
details.whyItMatters: Satellite internet constellations could bring broadband to the billions of people who lack it. Starlink represents a fundamental new approach to global connectivity.
takeaways: Starlink uses thousands of low-Earth orbit satellites
It provides broadband to areas without traditional infrastructure
Low orbit reduces latency compared to geostationary satellites

faq.question: How is Starlink different from traditional satellite internet?
faq.answer: Traditional satellite internet uses geostationary satellites 36,000 km above Earth, causing high latency. Starlink orbits at about 550 km, reducing round-trip latency to 20 to 40 milliseconds. The large constellation provides continuous coverage as satellites pass overhead.

faq.question: Can satellite internet replace terrestrial broadband?
faq.answer: Not in urban areas where fiber and cable offer higher capacity and lower cost. But for rural and remote areas, maritime, aviation, and disaster recovery, satellite is often the only viable option. It complements terrestrial networks rather than replacing them.
